concepts.title: Drainage Patterns and the Himalayan Rivers
concepts.definition: The drainage system of India follows the uplift of the Himalayas and the peninsular slope, showing dendritic, trellis, radial and rectangular patterns; the Himalayan rivers Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra are perennial, snow fed and form big basins with gorges, meanders and deltas.
concepts.key_idea: The Indus rises near Mansarovar with five tributaries of Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while the Ganga basin and Brahmaputra carry the largest water volume.

concepts.title: Peninsular Rivers, River Regimes and Pollution
concepts.definition: Peninsular rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Narmada and Tapi are rain fed and seasonal, flowing through hard rock terrain with estuaries instead of large deltas, and their flow regimes depend on the monsoon; rivers face pollution and inter-state disputes requiring water quality management.
concepts.key_idea: The east flowing rivers form deltas while the west flowing Narmada and Tapi occupy rift valleys making estuaries, which shows the structural control of peninsular drainage.

concepts.title: Important Rivers and Water Resources Management
concepts.definition: India's rivers carry about 1869 cubic km of water annually, and their basins support hydel power, irrigation and inland navigation, so water management through multipurpose projects, pollution control and inter-state cooperation is central to the drainage geography of the country.
concepts.key_idea: Multipurpose river valley projects like the Bhakra Nangal and Damodar Valley combine irrigation, power, flood control and navigation on the major river systems.
